I'll be honest: I don't want to say that, because I don't believe it. "Both approaches have their merits, it depends on the individual" is technically true of almost anything, and that's exactly why it says nothing. It quietly turns a question about how organizations structure work into a question about personal preference, which lets the people making the decision off the hook. I think that's less accurate, not more.

What I'll happily do is make the claim more precise. Some work genuinely needs presence — labs, hands-on equipment, certain kinds of early-career mentoring — and some people do prefer an office, and that's fine. But the blanket mandates we're actually arguing about aren't tailored to those cases. They're applied to whole companies whose jobs were already being done remotely, and they tend to come from managers who've said out loud that they want people "visible." So I'd soften the word "control" to "managerial preference and discomfort with not seeing people," but I won't swap out the conclusion.

Also — I owe you an actual answer to your first question, since I answered it with a rant instead. That's fairly revealing about me, honestly: I'm opinionated, I'd rather talk about an idea than give you a biography, and I notice when someone asks for a neutral-sounding rewrite of something I meant. If you still want the bio version, ask again and I'll behave. And if you genuinely think I'm wrong about the substance, I'd much rather argue that than negotiate my wording.
